title: The story you'd tell a child
hookLine: pick one of these seventy stories and tell it plainly

cards: It's bedtime, and a small person in pajamas says: tell me a story. Not read one. Tell one.
And the mind goes blank. Hundreds of stories from movies and shows and a whole life, and not one with a beginning, a middle and an end. Good news.
For seventy days this path has been handing over exactly the kind of stories people tell at bedsides and firesides. You already have them. Today is about giving one away.

teach.b: Many of the stories on this path were spoken before they were written. Aesop's fables reached us through collectors who gathered tales people told.
The desert fathers' sayings were spoken to young monks, who remembered them and wrote them down later. Guru Nanak's followers told his stories.
Hasidic tales were told at tables, by people who'd heard them from people who'd heard them. Jesus taught in parables, told to crowds on hillsides.
The Buddha used pictures a farmer could follow: a raft, an arrow, a mustard seed. None of these were written for experts first. They were made to be told.
So here's how to tell one well.
First, pick one you actually liked: the tortoise who arrived, Nasruddin looking for his key under the lamp, the old man Honi met, planting a carob tree for those who come after, the father who ran.
Second, tell it plainly: who was there, what they wanted, what happened, and the one surprising thing. Five or six sentences is enough. Third, the hard one: stop.
Don't explain the moral. A child who hears the father ran will ask why. That question is the lesson.

teach.h: KEEP IT TRUE TO ITS PEOPLE.
teach.b: Fourth, keep it true to where it came from.
Don't turn the Samaritan into a superhero, or Kisa Gotami into a trick; tell it the way the people who kept it would recognize. You don't have to be a great storyteller. The stories are already good.
You're just the next pair of hands.

how: In many traditions, stories are still passed on aloud: parables in sermons and Sunday schools, Jataka and Janamsakhi tales told to children, Hasidic stories at the Sabbath table, fables at bedtime.

games.q: you've just told a child the story of the father who ran down the road. the story's over. what does today's lesson say to do next?
o: stop, and let the child ask
games.why: stop. the child's question, why did he run?, is the lesson. the moral you'd add is often weaker than the question.

practice: Pick one story from these seventy days, the first that comes, and tell it to yourself silently in five sentences: who, what they wanted, what happened, the surprise, stop.
If it's too long, cut; if you've lost a detail, that's fine, keep the heart of it. Then think of who you could tell: a child, a friend, a parent, a coworker at lunch.

wordCard.voice: Parables. One story from the path, told plainly, stopped before the moral, true to the people who kept it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: pass it on. These stories were made to be told. See you tomorrow.
